kurals.tamil:
ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடாது இறைபுரிந்து யார்மாட்டும்
தேர்ந்துசெய் வஃதே முறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Orndhukan Notaadhu Iraipurindhu Yaarmaattum
Therndhusey Vaqdhe Murai.
kurals.meaning: Justice means looking into every case with care, showing no favour to anyone, holding to fairness, and acting only after the matter has been weighed with people who know the law.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a teacher who finds two kids fighting over a broken toy. A fair teacher doesn’t just blame the kid she likes less. She asks questions, listens to both, thinks it over, and then decides. Even if the one who broke it is her favourite helper, the rule is the same for him. That is what “doing it the right way” means.
kurals.university: This opening couplet works as a definition: முறை (justice, right order) is a four-step procedure. ஓர்ந்து means investigating what offence was committed; கண்ணோடாது means without கண்ணோட்டம், the soft favour that comes from familiarity or affection (Valluvar gives this quality its own chapter, 58, where it is praised in private life, which is why it has to be ruled out here); இறைபுரிந்து is glossed by Parimelazhagar as holding to impartiality (இறை = நடுவுநிலைமை), though some modern readers take இறை as ‘the ruler’ and the phrase as ‘the king, wishing it’; and தேர்ந்து செய்வது means deciding with those learned in the law books and then giving the fitting penalty. யார்மாட்டும் (‘with anyone at all’) governs the whole sequence, so a kinsman gets no exemption. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this procedural reading; Kalaignar compresses it to ‘not leaning to either side’. Parimelazhagar notes that the chapter follows பொச்சாவாமை (vigilance) and comes before its opposite, கொடுங்கோன்மை (Ch. 56); செங்கோல், the ‘straight sceptre’, is the standard Tamil metonym for just rule. ytamizh and Thirukkural.net give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A king should, without doubt, look upon his subjects as his own children. In determining their disputes, however, he should not show compassion.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that a king should love his people like a father, but that this love must not tip the scales when he judges their quarrels.
hinduism.tie_back: This is கண்ணோடாது exactly: when judgment is given, affection is set aside.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section LXIX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: both texts keep fatherly care for the people but explicitly exclude it from the act of judging.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to handle discipline in the church without favouring anyone.
christianity.tie_back: Doing nothing by partiality is the Kural’s ‘showing favour to no one’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on impartiality; the setting is church discipline, not a king’s court, and it says nothing about investigation.

islam.quote_or_event: “What destroyed the nations preceding you, was that if a noble amongst them stole, they would forgive him, and if a poor person amongst them stole, they would inflict Allah's Legal punishment on him. By Allah, if Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand.”
islam.explanation: When the Quraysh sent Usama to plead for a noblewoman who had stolen, the Prophet refused and declared that the law would apply even to his own daughter.
islam.tie_back: This is யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது, favour to no one, however close or high.
islam._accuracy_note: An almost exact match on refusing favouritism in judgment; the investigative steps of the Kural are not in view.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; ye shall hear the small and the great alike; ye shall not be afraid of the face of any man; for the judgment is God’s;”
judaism.explanation: Moses tells the judges of Israel to give poor and powerful the same hearing and to fear no one, since justice belongs to God.
judaism.tie_back: Hearing everyone alike and favouring no one is the same rule the Kural sets for the king.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on impartial hearing; the Kural adds consultation with the learned before sentencing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by passing arbitrary judgments does a man become just; a wise man is he who investigates both right and wrong. He who does not judge others arbitrarily, but passes judgment impartially according to the truth, that sagacious man is a guardian of law and is called just.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a judge is just only if he investigates both sides and decides impartially according to the truth, not on a whim.
buddhism.tie_back: Investigate (ஓர்ந்து), judge impartially (கண்ணோடாது), and so be called just (முறை): the two texts follow the same sequence.
buddhism._accuracy_note: An exceptionally close structural parallel: investigation followed by impartial judgment defines the just man.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth that closes Plato’s Gorgias, Zeus decrees that souls are to be judged after death stripped of body, wealth and rank, by judges who are themselves stripped, because in earlier times the clothed judges had been deceived by fine appearances and false witnesses; Minos, Rhadamanthus and Aeacus are appointed to judge.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows the gods reforming judgment so that nothing (status, beauty, supporters) can sway the verdict.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises கண்ணோடாது: a true verdict must look past whoever the person appears to be.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good thematic parallel on impartial judgment, but it concerns judgment of the dead, not a king’s earthly court.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “to go to the judge is to go to justice; for the nature of the judge is to be a sort of animate justice;”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says people in a dispute go to a judge because the judge is supposed to be justice itself in living form, standing at the fair midpoint between the parties.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks the king to be exactly this, the living ‘mean’ who leans to neither side.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.4, 1132a (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the judge as embodied impartial justice; Aristotle is analysing corrective justice, not giving a procedure.

kurals.tamil:
வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம் மன்னவன்
கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaanokki Vaazhum Ulakellaam Mannavan
Kolnokki Vaazhung Kuti.
kurals.meaning: Every living thing on earth looks to the sky for rain, and in the same way the people of a land look to their king’s sceptre, meaning his just rule, in order to live.
kurals.elementary: Plants in a garden wait for rain, and without it they dry up. The people of a country are a bit like that garden: they are waiting for their leaders to be fair and kind. When the leader rules well, it is like a good rain, and everyone grows.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on an exact parallel: வான் நோக்கி வாழும் உலகு (the world that lives looking to the sky) matches கோல் நோக்கி வாழும் குடி (the citizenry that lives looking to the sceptre). As commentators note, வான் here stands for rain by metonymy, which echoes the opening chapter on rain (வான்சிறப்பு, Ch. 2), where rain sustains all life. Parimelazhagar reads உலகெல்லாம் as ‘all living beings’ and குடி as the settled subjects of the kingdom. Just as he reads கோல் throughout the chapter, the sceptre means just rule, not simply power. Varadarasan and Pappaiah keep the rain comparison; Kalaignar makes it ‘good government is as necessary to citizens as rain is to living things’. The comparison already hints at 545 and 559 (in the next chapter), where just rule and rainfall are causally linked. Both sources agree on the text; வாழுங் is the sandhi form of வாழும் before குடி.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For, when these creatures, being without a king, through fear dispersed in all directions, the Lord created a king for the protection of this whole (creation),”
hinduism.explanation: Manu explains that kingship was created because, without a king, people scattered in fear and could not live securely.
hinduism.tie_back: The subjects ‘live looking to the sceptre’ because, without it, ordinary life cannot go on.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that people depend on the king for security, but lacks the rain comparison and the stress on justice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth. In his days shall the righteous flourish; and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm prays that the just king will be for his people what rain is to the cut grass, bringing new life and peace.
christianity.tie_back: The same picture as the Kural: the righteous ruler is to his people what rain is to the earth.
christianity._accuracy_note: A striking parallel: both compare the just king to rain on which life depends.

islam.quote_or_event: “Surely! Everyone of you is a guardian and is responsible for his charges: The Imam (ruler) of the people is a guardian and is responsible for his subjects;”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the ruler as a shepherd whose flock depends on him and for whom he must answer.
islam.tie_back: The flock looking to its shepherd matches the people looking to the sceptre.
islam._accuracy_note: Captures the people’s dependence on the ruler’s care; the rain image and the focus on justice are absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When the righteous are increased, the people rejoice; but when the wicked beareth rule, the people sigh.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says the people’s condition follows the character of those who rule them.
judaism.tie_back: Because the people’s welfare hangs on the ruler’s justice, they live ‘looking to the sceptre’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same dependence of the people on just rule, without the Kural’s cosmic rain comparison.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When cattle cross a river, if the bull goes straight, they all go straight, because their leader is straight. So it is for humans: when the one deemed chief does the right thing, what do you expect the rest to do? The whole nation sleeps at ease, when the king is just.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a people to a herd crossing a river that follows the lead bull, straight or crooked.
buddhism.tie_back: The whole nation ‘sleeps at ease’ under a just king, just as the people live by looking to the straight sceptre.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in substance, and ‘straight’ neatly echoes செங்கோல்; the image is a herd rather than rain.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “All the people look towards him while he settles causes with true judgements:”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the king favoured by the Muses, on whom the whole people fix their eyes as he gives straight verdicts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s own phrase: the people ‘look to’ the king (நோக்கி) as he judges rightly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Nearly verbal overlap on the people looking to the just judge-king; the rain comparison is missing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He is the bond which fastens the commonwealth together, he is the breath of life to all those thousands, who by themselves would become merely an encumbrance and a source of plunder if that directing mind were withdrawn”
philosophy.explanation: Writing to Nero, Seneca compares the ruler to the mind that directs the body and says the great multitude lives by him and would fall into ruin without him.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's image of all life looking to the rain, Seneca makes the ruler the very breath by which the people live.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 4 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Clemency, Book I). Strong match on the people's total dependence on the ruler; Seneca's image is breath and mind rather than rain, and his stress is on the ruler's direction rather than specifically on just rule.

kurals.tamil:
அந்தணர் நூற்கும் அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய்
நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Andhanar Noorkum Araththirkum Aadhiyaai
Nindradhu Mannavan Kol.
kurals.meaning: The king’s sceptre is the foundation that keeps both the scriptures of the sages and the dharma they teach standing.
kurals.elementary: Think of a town library. The books are wonderful, but if nobody keeps the doors safe and the roof mended, the books get ruined and people stop reading. A fair ruler is like the person who keeps the library safe, so that good teachings and good behaviour can last.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar takes அந்தணர் நூல் as the Vedas and அறம் as the dharma they lay down, and he explains ஆதியாய் நின்றது (‘stood as the origin’) causally: if the sceptre fails, the Veda is forgotten and dharma lapses, so the sceptre is their support, not their source in time. Varadarasan follows him (‘the scripture revered by the Brahmins’). Modern commentators widen the terms: Solomon Pappaiah reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who cultivate wisdom’ and நூல் as their books of knowledge, Kalaignar speaks of ‘the books of the virtuous’, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who know the end’. The couplet sets out a characteristic Kural view: learning and morality are not self-sustaining; they need a just political order to protect them. Pope’s ‘Learning and virtue of the sages spring / From all-controlling sceptre of the king’ overstates the idea of origin. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That sceptre on which the well-being and progress of the sciences of Anvikshaki, the triple Vedas, and Varta depend is known as Danda (punishment).”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya says the well-being of philosophy, the three Vedas and economic life all depend on the king’s sceptre of just punishment.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s thesis word for word: the Vedas and the order of life rest on the king’s கோல்.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Exceptionally close: both name the sceptre as what the Vedas and ordered life depend on.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks Christians to pray for rulers because stable government is what allows a godly and honest life.
christianity.tie_back: Religion and virtue flourish under the ruler’s protection, which is the Kural’s point.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that religious life depends on orderly rule; it does not call the ruler the foundation of scripture.

islam.quote_or_event: “We have already sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance that the people may maintain [their affairs] in justice. And We sent down iron, wherein is great military might and benefits for the people,”
islam.explanation: The verse puts scripture, the balance of justice and ‘iron’ (coercive power) side by side as the gifts that keep human society just.
islam.tie_back: Scripture needs the balance and the iron, just as the sages’ books and dharma need the sceptre.
islam._accuracy_note: Close structurally: revelation is linked with enforcing power in the service of justice; the order of priority differs, since in the Qur’an scripture comes first.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In all matters, his deeds shall be for the sake of heaven. His purpose and intent shall be to elevate the true faith and fill the world with justice, destroying the power of the wicked and waging the wars of God.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides defines the purpose of Jewish kingship as raising up the true faith and filling the world with justice.
judaism.tie_back: The king’s power exists to uphold religion and righteousness, as in the Kural.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 4:10 (trans. E. Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close: royal power is the support of faith and justice; Maimonides speaks of purpose rather than of foundation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta, the Buddha describes the duty of a wheel-turning monarch: relying on the Dhamma and honouring it, he is to provide righteous protection for his household, troops, nobles, brahmins and householders, town and country people, ascetics and brahmins, and even animals and birds, and to allow no wrongdoing in his realm.
buddhism.explanation: The ideal king’s protective rule makes room for recluses and brahmins to live out their spiritual life.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the righteous ruler the guardian under whom teachers of dharma can flourish.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit on the protective role; the sutta places the Dhamma above the king rather than resting on him.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles swears by the sceptre that the sons of the Achaeans carry in their hands when they give judgment, the men who guard the ordinances (themistes) that come from Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer the sceptre is the visible sign that the judge-king holds and protects the god-given laws.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The sceptre as guardian of sacred law is close to the Kural’s கோல் upholding scripture and dharma.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear image of the sceptre as keeper of divine law; the passage is an oath, not a claim that learning depends on it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But justice is the bond of men in states, for the administration of justice, which is the determination of what is just, is the principle of order in political society.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that people without law and justice are the most savage of animals, and that the administration of justice is what holds a state together.
philosophy.tie_back: For both writers, justice administered by the ruler is the foundation on which the rest of human goodness stands.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘justice as foundation’ idea but does not mention scriptures or sages.

kurals.tamil:
குடிதழீஇக் கோலோச்சும் மாநில மன்னன்
அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kutidhazheeik Kolochchum Maanila Mannan
Atidhazheei Nirkum Ulaku.
kurals.meaning: The world stays clinging to the feet of the great king who rules while embracing his people.
kurals.elementary: A team captain who looks after every player, helping the slow ones and cheering up the scared ones, ends up with a team that would follow her anywhere. People hold on to a leader who holds on to them first.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a chiasmus of the verb தழுவு (embrace), used twice in the lengthened form தழீஇ: the king embraces the people (குடி தழீஇ), and the world embraces his feet (அடி தழீஇ). The long vowel (இசைநிறை அளபெடை) fills out the metre and gives the word emphasis. கோல் ஓச்சுதல், ‘wielding the sceptre’, is the idiom for ruling. Parimelazhagar explains ‘embracing the subjects’ as protecting them with love and learning what they lack; ‘clinging to his feet’ means the world will not leave him, so his kingdom stands firm. Varadarasan: ‘the world holds fast to the feet of the king who rules embracing his people with love’. Pappaiah turns it into people living ‘around the feet’ of such a ruler, and Kalaignar has the whole earth honouring the footsteps of a good government. In சுற்றந்தழால் (Ch. 53) Valluvar used the same verb for embracing kin; here the embrace is extended to the whole people. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In the happiness of his subjects lies his happiness; in their welfare his welfare; whatever pleases himself he shall not consider as good, but whatever pleases his subjects he shall consider as good.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya tells the king to treat his people’s happiness and welfare as his own.
hinduism.tie_back: This is what குடி தழீஇ means in practice: the king takes the people’s good as his own.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on the embrace of the people; it lacks the second half, the world’s answering loyalty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts rulers who lord it over others with his own rule, that the greatest must be the servant of all.
christianity.tie_back: Greatness that comes from serving the people is the kind the Kural says the world will cling to.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ruler-as-servant idea; it is addressed to disciples, not to kings, and does not promise loyalty in return.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best of your rulers are those whom you love and who love you, who invoke God's blessings upon you and you invoke His blessings upon them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes the best rulers as those bound to their people in mutual love and prayer.
islam.tie_back: This is the same two-way embrace: the ruler holds the people and the people hold the ruler.
islam._accuracy_note: A very close match to the Kural’s mutual embrace between ruler and ruled.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The elders advise the young king Rehoboam that if he serves the people kindly, they will be loyal to him for ever; he rejects their advice and loses most of the kingdom.
judaism.tie_back: The same promise as the Kural: embrace the people and they will cling to you for good.
judaism._accuracy_note: A near-exact conditional parallel: serve the people and their lasting loyalty follows.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All men are my children. What I desire for my own children, and I desire their welfare and happiness both in this world and the next, that I desire for all men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist emperor Ashoka tells his judicial officers that he wants every subject’s welfare as a father wants his children’s.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka’s paternal embrace of all subjects is the குடி தழீஇ ideal carved in stone.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Kalinga Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on the ruler’s embrace; the people’s answering devotion is implied, not stated.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Ithacan assembly, Mentor protests that no one now remembers Odysseus, who ruled his people gently, like a father, and bitterly suggests that kings might as well be harsh and unjust from now on.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus is held up as the model king who treated his people like a father, and the people’s forgetfulness is condemned.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s ideal, the king who embraces his people, and complains when the loyalty that should follow is missing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear picture of the fatherly king; the passage laments that loyalty failed, the reverse of the Kural’s promise.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “That man's greatness alone rests upon a secure foundation, whom all men know to be as much on their side as he is above them … at whose approach they do not fly in terror, as though some evil and dangerous animal had sprung out from its den, but flock to him as they would to the bright and health-giving sunshine.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca adds that the subjects of such a ruler guard his sleep, surround and defend him, and offer their own bodies to protect him.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler who stands on his people's side is held fast by them, as the Kural's world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 3 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Clemency, Book I); the ellipsis omits a clause about the ruler's daily care for his subjects' safety. Close match on the reciprocity of a caring ruler and devoted subjects.

kurals.tamil:
இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும் மன்னவன் நாட்ட
பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Iyalpulik Kolochchum Mannavan Naatta
Peyalum Vilaiyulum Thokku.
kurals.meaning: In the land of a king who rules by the proper law, seasonal rain and rich harvests are found together.
kurals.elementary: When a family shares fairly and nobody grabs, dinner time is happy and there is enough for everyone. The old Tamil poets believed a whole country works that way: when the ruler is fair, even the rain and the crops seem to join in.
kurals.university: இயல்புளி is இயல்பு with the instrumental ending உளி (= ஆல்), ‘by the proper nature/way’. Parimelazhagar glosses it as ruling according to the method laid down in the books of statecraft (நீதிநூல்), and Varadarasan (‘நீதி முறைப்படி’) and Pappaiah (‘அரச நீதிநூல்கள் கூறியபடி’) follow him. நாட்ட is a genitive plural predicate, ‘belong to his land’. பெயல் is seasonal rainfall and விளையுள் the abundant yield. The final தொக்கு (having gathered together) means the two are always found together there. Behind the couplet lies a belief found across ancient cultures, that the king’s righteousness governs the fertility of the land. Valluvar states the negative in the next chapter: முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல் (559). Kalaignar reads it as a simile, that just government is like timely rain bringing a good harvest, which softens the causal claim. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whether it is the king that makes the age, or, it is the age that makes the king, is a question about which thou shouldst not entertain any doubt. The truth is that the king makes the age.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches that when the king rules fully by the science of just punishment the Krita age sets in and the earth yields crops in abundance, while under an unjust king the clouds do not pour seasonably and crops fail.
hinduism.tie_back: The same causal chain as the Kural: righteous rule brings rain and harvest together.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section LXIX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: the same section explicitly ties seasonable rain and crops to the king’s just rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment. … Then judgment shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah foresees a righteous king, and a time when justice and righteousness make even the wilderness fruitful.
christianity.tie_back: Just rule and fruitful land belong together, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared link between righteous rule and fertility; in Isaiah the fruitfulness follows an outpouring of the spirit, not the king alone.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if only the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied [the messengers], so We seized them for what they were earning.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says a community’s faith and God-consciousness would open blessings from sky and earth.
islam.tie_back: Blessings from heaven (rain) and earth (harvest) depend on moral order, as in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on moral order bringing sky-and-earth blessing; it concerns the community’s faith, not the ruler’s justice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If ye walk in My statutes, and keep My commandments, and do them; then I will give your rains in their season, and the land shall yield her produce, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah promises rain in season and a full harvest if Israel lives by God’s laws.
judaism.tie_back: Rain in season and yield together, as a reward for living by the law, is the Kural’s பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in the pairing of seasonal rain and harvest; the condition is the nation’s obedience, not the king’s rule.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “At a time when kings are principled, royal officials become principled. … the heavens provide plenty of rain. When the heavens provide plenty of rain, the crops ripen well.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces a chain from righteous kings through officials and people to regular seasons, good rain and ripening crops.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s claim itself: a principled king means good rain and good harvest together.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-perfect match: the king’s righteousness leads causally to rain and ripe crops.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it: … The earth bears them victual in plenty, and on the mountains the oak bears acorns upon the top and bees in the midst.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that Zeus rewards cities whose judges give straight verdicts with peace and a generous earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: ‘Straight judgements’ are the Greek செங்கோல், and plenty from the earth follows, just as in the Kural.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225–233 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close: straight justice by rulers is tied directly to the fertility of the land.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But those officers whose land he sees lying idle and with but few inhabitants, owing either to the harshness of their government, their insolence, or their neglect, he punishes, and making them to cease from their office he appoints other rulers in their place.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells Critobulus that the Persian king rewards governors whose districts are thickly peopled and richly cultivated, and removes those whose land lies waste through harsh or careless rule.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Xenophon ties the fruitfulness of a land to the quality of its government, though through administration rather than seasonal rain.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus (The Economist), ch. IV, 8 (tr. H. G. Dakyns)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Dakyns' translation on Project Gutenberg (eBook #1173). Partial match: the link between good government and abundant harvests is explicit, but it works through policy and oversight, with no cosmic or seasonal element.

kurals.tamil:
வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது மன்னவன்
கோலதூஉங் கோடா தெனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Velandru Vendri Tharuvadhu Mannavan
Koladhooung Kotaa Thenin.
kurals.meaning: It is not the spear that brings a king victory but his sceptre, provided that the sceptre does not bend.
kurals.elementary: A kid who wins a game by cheating doesn’t really win, because soon nobody wants to play with him. A kid who plays fair keeps her friends and keeps winning. For a ruler too, being fair is stronger than being scary.
kurals.university: The couplet sets வேல் (spear, the emblem of military force) against கோல் (sceptre, the emblem of justice), two words that differ by a single consonant. அதூஉம், the lengthened form of அதுவும் (‘that too’, with அளபெடை), adds a condition: the sceptre gives victory only if it too does not bend (கோடாது எனின்). The verb கோடு, ‘to bend, be crooked’, is the root of கொடுங்கோல் (tyranny, Ch. 56). Parimelazhagar explains that the spear wins only because the subjects stand loyally with a just king, so victory really comes from the sceptre and the spear is its instrument. Varadarasan and Pappaiah agree; Kalaignar makes the contrast explicit: not the spear that fells enemies, but the unbending sceptre that lets the people live. The point anticipates the chapters on the army (77–78), which treat military strength as dependent on the loyalty that just rule creates. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.explanation: Vyasa reminds Gandhari that for all eighteen days of the war, when Duryodhana begged her to bless his victory, she replied only that victory lies where righteousness is; the righteous side won.
hinduism.tie_back: Victory follows dharma, not arms: the sceptre, not the spear, as the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Section 14 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A very close match on victory flowing from righteousness rather than force; this maxim is famous in Sanskrit as yato dharmas tato jayaḥ.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist says a king’s safety does not come from the size of his army.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it denies that military force is what secures a king.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the denial of military power; the psalm points to God’s care rather than to the king’s justice.

islam.quote_or_event: The jurist Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) is widely quoted as teaching that God upholds a just state even if it is unbelieving, and does not uphold an unjust state even if it is Muslim, because the world can endure with justice joined to unbelief but not with injustice joined to faith.
islam.explanation: A major Islamic legal thinker makes justice, rather than power or even religious label, the thing that keeps a state standing.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point: a state’s lasting success depends on a straight sceptre.
islam.source: Ibn Taymiyya, as cited from Majmu‘ al-Fatawa and his writings on public order (hisba)
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit, but it is a medieval jurist’s maxim known through secondary citation, not scripture, and is paraphrased here.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet tells Zerubbabel that the Temple will be rebuilt not by force but by God’s spirit.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts reject force as what really decides success.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the rejection of might, but credits divine spirit rather than just rule; a looser parallel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Now it is conquest by Dhamma that Beloved-of-the-Gods considers to be the best conquest.”
buddhism.explanation: After the slaughter of the Kalinga war, Ashoka renounced conquest by arms and declared that conquest by righteousness is the best kind.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka discovered in practice what the Kural states: victory by the sceptre, not by the spear.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match of righteousness over arms as the true source of victory.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the son of Cronos has ordained this law for men, that fishes and beasts and winged fowls should devour one another, for right is not in them; but to mankind he gave right which proves far the best.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother to give up violence, because Zeus gave humans justice, which proves far better than the rule of force among animals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Right proving ‘far the best’ over force is the Kural’s preference for the sceptre over the spear.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 276–280 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shares justice-over-force, but concerns human life in general rather than a king’s victory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But, of all motives, none is better adapted to secure influence and hold it fast than love; nothing is more foreign to that end than fear.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that no amount of armed power can withstand the hatred of the many, as the fate of tyrants shows, while the affection won by just rule keeps power safe for ever.
philosophy.tie_back: Lasting victory comes from just rule that wins the people, not from force, which is the Kural's sceptre set above the spear.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §23 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, De Officiis II.1-43). Strong match on force versus the goodwill that just rule earns; Cicero speaks of holding power rather than winning wars.

kurals.tamil:
இறைகாக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் அவனை
முறைகாக்கும் முட்டாச் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Iraikaakkum Vaiyakam Ellaam Avanai
Muraikaakkum Muttaach Cheyin.
kurals.meaning: The king guards the whole world, and justice guards the king, as long as he administers it without fail.
kurals.elementary: If you always tell the truth and treat your friends fairly, then when someone spreads a nasty rumour about you, your friends stand up for you. Your fairness becomes your shield. It works the same way for rulers.
kurals.university: The two halves mirror each other with the verb காக்கும் (guards): இறை காக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் (the lord guards the whole world) and அவனை முறை காக்கும் (justice guards him). The condition முட்டாச் செயின், ‘if he does it without lapse’ (முட்டு = obstruction, failure), is the hinge. Parimelazhagar explains that the merit of just rule protects the king from harm that would otherwise come to him; Varadarasan: ‘if he rules without harming justice, that justice itself protects him’. Pappaiah reads முட்டா as qualifying முறை, i.e. ‘his flawless, upright rule protects him’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the condition oddly (‘even if they err’), which the grammar does not support. The idea is the political counterpart of the Aram principle that dharma protects those who protect it; compare Manu’s ‘dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ’. Both sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches the classic principle dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ: justice protects those who protect it and destroys those who violate it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘justice guards him who does not fail it’ is the same maxim.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; Manu frames it for judges, the Kural for the king.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb promises a lasting throne to the king who judges the poor faithfully.
christianity.tie_back: Just judgment secures the king himself, which is the Kural’s point.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close: justice given by the king becomes the guarantee of his own throne.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will give shade, to seven, on the Day when there will be no shade but His. (These seven persons are) a just ruler, …”
islam.explanation: First among the seven whom God shelters on the Day of Judgment is the just ruler.
islam.tie_back: The ruler’s justice becomes his protection, here in the next world.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on justice sheltering the ruler; the protection is eschatological, not political.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness; For the throne is established by righteousness.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb holds that a king’s throne is made firm by righteousness, not by wickedness.
judaism.tie_back: Righteousness upholding the throne is justice guarding the king.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close: justice is what secures the ruler’s position.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dhamma surely protects one who practices Dhamma.”
buddhism.explanation: The elder Dhammika teaches that Dhamma, well practised, protects the one who practises it and brings happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to the king: practise justice and justice guards you.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The same principle in general form; not specific to kingship.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Next he married bright Themis who bare the Horae (Hours), and Eunomia (Order), Dike (Justice), and blooming Eirene (Peace), who mind the works of mortal men,”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod makes Order, Justice and Peace daughters of Zeus and Themis who watch over human affairs.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Justice as a guardian power watching over those who honour it gives the Kural’s idea a mythic form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weaker match: Justice as a divine guardian, but with no stated promise to protect a just king.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that of all means of gaining and keeping power, none is better suited than being loved and none worse than being feared; fear, he says, is a poor guardian of lasting power, while goodwill keeps it safe for ever, and he points to the violent ends of tyrants.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, a ruler’s best protection is the goodwill won by just and generous conduct, not guards or terror.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler who guards others justly is himself guarded, as the Kural says.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong thematic parallel, paraphrased; Cicero stresses goodwill rather than justice as an impersonal force.

kurals.tamil:
எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
தண்பதத்தான் தானே கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enpadhaththaan Oraa Muraiseyyaa Mannavan
Thanpadhaththaan Thaane Ketum.
kurals.meaning: A king whom his people cannot easily reach, who does not look into their complaints and give justice, sinks low and perishes by his own doing, even without an enemy.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a class monitor who locks herself away and never listens when kids come to her with a problem. Problems pile up, everyone gets upset, and soon nobody trusts her. She didn’t need an enemy to lose her job. She lost it all by herself.
kurals.university: எண்பதம் means ‘easy access’ (எண் = easy, பதம் = occasion or audience; Varadarasan: எளிய செவ்வி); தண்பதம் means a ‘low state’ (Parimelazhagar: தாழ்ந்த நிலை). The two rhyming compounds frame the couplet. Commentators take the negation of ஓரா (not examining) and முறைசெய்யா (not doing justice) as extending back over எண்பதத்தான், so the king is one who is not accessible, does not investigate, and does not give justice; Pope accordingly renders ‘Hard of access, nought searching out’. Pappaiah keeps the positive reading grammatically but gives the same sense. தானே கெடும் (‘perishes of himself’) is taken by Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan to mean ‘even without enemies’ (பகைவரில்லாமலும்): neglect of justice is self-destruction. Kalaignar departs and reads எண்பதம் as pomp or display. The couplet links accessibility to justice, a theme taken up again in வெருவந்தசெய்யாமை (Ch. 57). The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Uttara Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Rama tells Lakshmana the story of King Nriga, who left two brahmins disputing over a cow waiting at his palace gate for days without a hearing; in their anger they cursed him to live as a lizard in a pit, and Rama draws the lesson that a king must never keep those seeking justice waiting.
hinduism.explanation: A king ruined not by an enemy but by his own failure to give petitioners a hearing.
hinduism.tie_back: Nriga is the Kural’s inaccessible king who ‘perishes of himself’.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (the story of Nriga, told by Rama)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Excellent thematic fit; details vary between recensions, and the Mahabharata version of Nriga stresses a disputed cow-gift rather than inaccessibility.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that whoever refuses to hear the poor will one day cry out and not be heard himself.
christianity.tie_back: The ruler who shuts out petitioners brings about his own downfall, as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on the self-inflicted consequence of not hearing complaints; not specific to kings.

islam.quote_or_event: “If Allah puts anyone in the position of authority over the affairs of the Muslims, and he secludes himself (from them), not fulfilling their needs, wants, and poverty, Allah will keep Himself away from him, not fulfilling his need, want and poverty.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that a ruler who shuts himself off from his people’s needs will find God shut off from his own; on hearing it, Mu‘awiya appointed a man to attend to people’s needs.
islam.tie_back: An almost exact counterpart of the Kural’s inaccessible ruler who ruins himself.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 2948 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Near-perfect match on the ruler’s seclusion from petitioners and its self-inflicted penalty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.”
judaism.explanation: Absalom stood at the city gate telling every litigant that King David had no one to hear his case, and so ‘stole the hearts’ of Israel and raised a revolt.
judaism.tie_back: A king’s failure to hear cases nearly costs David his throne, without any foreign enemy, just as the Kural warns.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; Absalom’s claim is self-serving, but the story shows the danger the Kural names.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore your aim should be to act with impartiality. … Those who are bored with the administration of justice will not be promoted;”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka warns his judicial officers that indifference, laziness and weariness lead to unjust imprisonment, and that those bored with justice will not advance.
buddhism.tie_back: Neglecting to examine cases and give justice is the fault the Kural condemns.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Kalinga Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the condemnation of neglected justice; addressed to officials, and the king’s self-ruin is not in view.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer compares the rout of the Trojans to the autumn storm that Zeus sends against men who give crooked judgments in the assembly and drive out justice, heedless of the gods, so that the rivers flood and the works of men are ruined.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, a community’s neglect of justice brings destruction without any human enemy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ruin that comes from within, through crooked judgment, is the Kural’s தானே கெடும்.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good on self-caused ruin through injustice; the passage is a simile about communities, not a single king’s inaccessibility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “An old woman once assailed Demetrius as he was passing by, and demanded many times that he give her a hearing. ‘I have no time,’ said Demetrius. ‘Then don't be king,’ screamed the old woman.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch says Demetrius was hard to approach, kept embassies waiting for years and threw his subjects' petitions into a river, so that the Macedonians felt insulted rather than ruled; soon afterwards his army deserted him and he lost Macedonia.
philosophy.tie_back: The king who cannot be reached and will not hear complaints undoes his own kingdom, exactly as the Kural warns.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Demetrius, ch. 42 (tr. Bernadotte Perrin)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Perrin, Loeb 1920); inner double quotation marks rendered as single quotes. Near one-to-one: inaccessibility and neglect of justice, followed by the loss of the kingdom through the subjects' desertion (ch. 44), though rival kings also attacked him.

kurals.tamil:
குடிபுறங் காத்தோம்பிக் குற்றம் கடிதல்
வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kutipurang Kaaththompik Kutram Katidhal
Vatuvandru Vendhan Thozhil.
kurals.meaning: Guarding the people from outside harm, caring for them, and curbing crime by punishment is no blemish on a king; it is his proper work.
kurals.elementary: A lifeguard who blows her whistle at kids running by the pool isn’t being mean. It is her job, keeping everyone safe. A fair ruler who stops people from doing wrong is doing the same kind of job.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar separates two kinds of protection: புறம் காத்து, guarding the people from others (enemies, robbers, grasping officials), and ஓம்பி, protecting them from himself (for example, by not over-taxing). Only then comes குற்றம் கடிதல், removing crime by fitting punishment. வடு அன்று (‘not a scar or blemish’) answers an implied objection that punishment, as a form of harm, conflicts with the ethic of non-injury taught in the Aram section (e.g. Ch. 32–33); வேந்தன் தொழில் (‘the king’s work’) makes it a duty of office. Varadarasan follows Parimelazhagar closely. Pappaiah reads குற்றம் as the people’s grievances (குறைகள்), which shifts the emphasis from punishment to redress. Kalaignar adds that the ruler should punish whoever the offender is, without fearing reproach. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads புறம் as ‘beyond the borders’. The couplet prepares for the harsher 550. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A king who punishes those who do not deserve it, and punishes not those who deserve it, brings great infamy on himself and (after death) sinks into hell.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu says that failing to punish the guilty disgraces a king as much as punishing the innocent.
hinduism.tie_back: The blemish lies in not punishing, which is the reverse side of the Kural’s ‘punishment is no blemish’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close: both deny that just punishment stains the king; Manu adds that failing to punish is itself infamy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. … for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that the ruler’s sword against evildoers is part of his God-given service, not a wrong.
christianity.tie_back: Punishing wrongdoing is the ruler’s proper work, not a stain, as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: the ruler’s punishment of evil is defended as legitimate duty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an treats authority as a trust and just judgment as a command from God.
islam.tie_back: Judging and correcting wrongdoing is a sacred duty of those in authority, not a fault.
islam._accuracy_note: Supports judgment as a duty; it does not directly address whether punishment stains the ruler.

judaism.quote_or_event: “pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina teaches that the fear government inspires is what stops people from devouring one another.
judaism.tie_back: The ruler’s power to restrain wrongdoers is a blessing to pray for, not a blemish.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the legitimacy of government restraint; it does not mention the ruler’s duty to guard from outside.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is my desire that there should be uniformity in law and uniformity in sentencing. I even go this far, to grant a three-day stay for those in prison who have been tried and sentenced to death.”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka, a Buddhist king, kept courts and punishments but insisted on uniform law and granted a reprieve for appeals.
buddhism.tie_back: Even a king devoted to non-harm accepts punishment as part of his work, as the Kural says, while tempering it.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Pillar Edict IV (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shows punishment as a duty of just rule; Ashoka’s emphasis on mercy is softer than the Kural.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena founds the court of the Areopagus and urges the Athenians not to banish all fear from their city, since no mortal who fears nothing remains just; the court is to be a guardian of the land, awake while others sleep.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess of wisdom establishes lawful punishment as the city’s protection.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Justice that restrains crime is presented as a gift to the city, not a stain, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong mythic parallel on legitimate, protective punishment; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But he who desires to inflict rational punishment does not retaliate for a past wrong which cannot be undone; he has regard to the future, and is desirous that the man who is punished, and he who sees him punished, may be deterred from doing wrong again.”
philosophy.explanation: Protagoras argues that rational punishment is not revenge but a way of protecting the future by deterring wrongdoing.
philosophy.tie_back: Punishment understood as protection is the Kural’s குற்றம் கடிதல் as the king’s duty.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in justifying punishment as protective; not specific to the king’s office.

kurals.tamil:
கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் பைங்கூழ்
களைகட் டதனொடு நேர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kolaiyir Kotiyaarai Vendhoruththal Paingoozh
Kalaikat Tadhanotu Ner.
kurals.meaning: For a king to punish violent criminals with death is like a farmer pulling up weeds to save the green crop.
kurals.elementary: A gardener pulls out weeds not because she hates plants but because the weeds would choke the vegetables. The Kural says a ruler must stop people who seriously hurt others, so that everyone else can grow up safe. (Grown-ups still argue about how harsh such punishments should be.)
kurals.university: The final couplet puts the chapter’s argument about punishment in an agricultural image: பைங்கூழ் is the young green crop, and களை கட்டல் is weeding. The phrase கொலையிற் கொடியாரை is read in two ways. Varadarasan and Pappaiah take கொலையின் as instrumental, so the king punishes the cruel ‘by death’ (கொலைத்தண்டனையால்). Kalaignar takes it as the offence, so the cruel are ‘those who commit murder and similar cruelties’. Parimelazhagar’s commentary follows the first line of reading and presents capital punishment as the protection of the good, just as the weed is removed for the crop’s sake. Commentators note the tension with the Aram section’s உயிர் கொல்லாமை (not killing, Ch. 33). The usual resolution is that Aram states the individual’s ethic while Porul states the king’s duty. Modern readers such as Kalaignar keep the metaphor but stress that it applies to hardened offenders, not the ordinary wrongdoer. The next chapter, Tyranny, reverses the image. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya calls the whole book of the Arthashastra devoted to criminal justice Kantakasodhana, ‘The Removal of Thorns’, treating the suppression of the wicked, the seizure of criminals and their trial as clearing thorns out of the realm.
hinduism.explanation: Indian statecraft pictured criminals as thorns that a king must root out so that his people can move and work safely.
hinduism.tie_back: Thorns removed from the realm and weeds pulled from the crop are the same kind of image.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book IV, ‘The Removal of Thorns’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in its plant-clearing image for punishing criminals; the book covers all crime, not only capital cases.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A wise king scattereth the wicked, and bringeth the wheel over them.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb uses the image of a threshing wheel: a wise king separates out the wicked as grain is separated from chaff.
christianity.tie_back: A farming image for the king’s removal of evildoers, as in the Kural’s weeding.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in its agricultural image of the king purging the wicked; threshing rather than weeding.

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is for you in legal retribution [saving of] life, O you [people] of understanding, that you may become righteous.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that lawful retribution for murder actually preserves life in the community.
islam.tie_back: Punishing killers to protect the living is the logic of weeding to save the crop.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in reasoning, that capital punishment protects the community; there is no plant image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Morning by morning will I destroy all the wicked of the land; to cut off all the workers of iniquity from the city of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: In this royal psalm the king vows to purge the land of evildoers every day.
judaism.tie_back: The king ‘cutting off’ the wicked to keep the city whole matches the Kural’s weeding.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the king’s duty to cut off the violent; later Jewish law greatly restricted capital punishment in practice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells of a king whose realm was plagued by bandits; his wise chaplain advises that execution, imprisonment and banishment will not end the plague, and that instead the king should give seed and fodder to farmers, capital to traders and proper wages to officials, after which the country became peaceful.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist text answers crime by removing its economic causes rather than by killing offenders.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a deliberate counterpoint: where the Kural pulls the weed, the sutta improves the soil so that weeds do not grow.
buddhism._accuracy_note: A contrasting rather than agreeing text, chosen because Buddhism has no close endorsement of capital punishment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And further, make a law by my order, that he who has no part in reverence and justice shall be put to death, for he is a plague of the state.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Protagoras’ myth, Zeus sends Hermes to give reverence and justice to all people, and orders that anyone who cannot share in them be put to death as a disease of the city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Removing one who destroys the community to save the rest is the Kural’s weeding in divine terms.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close in its justification of capital punishment to protect the community; the image is disease rather than weeds.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the good physician and lawgiver of the State ought, like the wise bee-master, to keep them at a distance and prevent, if possible, their ever coming in; and if they have anyhow found a way in, then he should have them and their cells cut out as speedily as possible.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato likens the lawgiver who removes the city’s destructive ‘drones’ to a beekeeper cutting diseased cells out of the hive.
philosophy.tie_back: Cutting out what harms the hive is the same move as pulling weeds from the crop.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in its natural image of removing harmful members; Plato speaks of a whole class of idlers, not of murderers.
